archetype.name: Lottery Team (shot-making, possession-losing)
archetype.definition: A team that shoots well enough to compete but gives away too many possessions through turnovers and missed rebounds, and is too soft at the rim to climb out of the West's bottom third without fixing that.

report.headline: Playoff-grade shooting, lottery-grade possessions: why the Clippers sit at 4-8
report.take:
The Clippers are 4-8, fourth in the Pacific and 21st on the site. The underlying numbers back that up rather than excuse it. Their Net Rtg of -4.1 ranks 20th, and the offense and defense both rank 21st. This follows a slide that was already under way: 50-32 two seasons ago, 42-40 and 19th on the site last year, and now a pace of 27 wins. The record is not a fluke of close games. The point differential implies 5 wins against the actual 4, so the W vs Pt Diff of -1 is close to noise. This is roughly what the team has played like.

The interesting part is how a team that shoots this well ends up with a below-average offense. Their eFG % of 55.1 ranks 9th, their TS % of 59 ranks 8th, and they hit 39.1% from three, 3rd in the league and well above its 35.2% average. Yet the ORtg is 112.2, 21st. They lose the possession game. Their TOV % of 15.7 is 29th, their ORB % of 24.2 is 25th, and they pull down 40.2 rebounds a game, 28th. Good shots are worth less when there are fewer of them. On the other end, the problem is the paint. Opponents shoot 69.2% at the rim, 27th and well above the league's 65.1, and they get there often, with an Opp Rim Rate that ranks 24th. That fits a frontcourt graded D-.

The raw numbers hide some movement and some individual problems. October was ugly: 1-4 while scoring 105.4 a game. In November the offense jumped to 117.29 a game, and the last five games have been essentially even, +0.2 per game, at 3-2, including a one-point win over OKC. The defense did not come along, though. They allowed 119.86 a game in November and 118 over the last five. Two rotation pieces are dragging the lineup down. Darius Garland carries a 29.2 USG % on efficient 60.1 TS %, yet his BPM is -3 and the team is 29.3 points per 100 worse with him on the floor. That On-Off is extreme and noisy over 12 games, but it is not a good sign for the player using the most possessions. Rui Hachimura is at 47.6 TS % with a -5.9 BPM, ranked 81st of 88 on his tab. Meanwhile the secondary guards are winning their minutes: Kris Dunn (+1.6 BPM), Kobe Sanders (+13 On-Off) and Keaton Wagler (+8.1).

Where does it go? Two forces pull in opposite directions. The 39.1% three-point shooting is higher than any of the last five seasons, which topped out at 38.1, so expect it to cool. The 15.7 TOV % is also far worse than the 12-13.4 range of those seasons, so expect it to improve. The defense, though, looks like last year's 116.1 DRtg team with worse rim protection, and that is the part least likely to fix itself. This is a low-30s-win team unless the frontcourt changes.

strengths.title: Elite shot-making from the perimeter
strengths.body: They hit 39.1% from three, 3rd in the league, on an average share of threes, and their eFG % ranks 9th. The core of it is real: this franchise has shot 36.8-38.1% from deep for five straight seasons, and Derrick Jones Jr. (67.4 TS %) and Brook Lopez (61.6) are finishing efficiently. Some regression from 39.1 is likely, but this should stay an above-average shooting team.

strengths.title: Supporting guards winning their minutes
strengths.body: Dunn ranks 19th of 109 on the shooting-guard tab with a positive BPM. Sanders and Wagler post big positive On-Off numbers despite modest box scores, so the bench backcourt has been a plus. Lopez (+8.9 On-Off, 0.7 BPM) is the one frontcourt player clearly helping. This is the kind of depth that keeps games close when the top usage options struggle.

strengths.title: Offense waking up in November
strengths.body: Scoring rose from 105.4 a game in October to 117.29 in November. The last five games have run at 118.2, nearly six points above the season average. Part of that is the shooting, and part is simply a slow start washing out. It is the main reason the recent results are near break-even.

concerns.title: Losing the possession battle
concerns.body: A 15.7 TOV % (29th) and a 24.2 ORB % (25th) mean the Clippers get far fewer shots than their opponents. That is why top-10 shooting produces a 21st-ranked offense. The turnovers look fixable, since they are well out of line with this team's history. The rebounding does not: RPG was 40.6 last year too.

concerns.title: No resistance at the rim
concerns.body: Opponents shoot 69.2% within four feet (27th) and take a large share of their shots there (24th), well above the league on both. With the frontcourt graded D- and opponent eFG % 26th, this is structural rather than variance. It is also getting worse, not better: the last five games have allowed more than the season average.

concerns.title: Two big-minute players underwater
concerns.body: Garland uses the most possessions on the team, yet carries a -3 BPM and a -29.3 On-Off. Hachimura is shooting 47.6 TS % with a -5.9 BPM. Twelve games make On-Off especially noisy. Still, when the lead ball-handler and the starting power forward both grade this poorly, the rotation's minutes distribution is costing them.

trend.note: A 1-4 October and a seven-game losing streak gave way to a 3-2 run with a near-even margin, driven by much better offense. The defense has slipped at the same time, so the climb is modest.

weekAhead.headline: Utah at home, then a three-game road trip through Texas
weekAhead.body:
The week opens with the softest game on the schedule: Utah at home. The Jazz are 1-13 with the league's 29th-ranked ORtg, and they barely force turnovers (Opp TOV % 26th), a welcome break for the Clippers' sloppiest habit. Then come three straight road games. San Antonio (12-2, Net Rtg 13, defense 3rd) and Houston (11-3, offense 2nd) are both clearly better teams. Dallas (7-7, Net Rtg 18th) is a near peer whose record slightly flatters it.

Splitting the four would be a decent result. Utah and Dallas are the winnable pair. The Spurs and Rockets attack exactly where the Clippers are weakest: the glass and the paint. The one lever against San Antonio is shooting, since the Spurs allow opponents 38.2% from three (28th).

keyMatchups.title: Garland against Utah's leaky point-guard defense
keyMatchups.body: Utah gives up the most to point guards relative to their usual output of any team in the league. That sets up Garland, who leads the Clippers in usage, to have a big night. A strong game would also test whether his ugly On-Off is noise or something real.

keyMatchups.title: Clippers' threes against Spurs' paint wall
keyMatchups.body: San Antonio protects the rim at a 3rd-ranked 59.5% and leads the league in rebounds per game. Little will come easily inside. The Spurs do concede 38.2% from three, though, and that is where the league's 3rd-best shooting team has to win the game.

keyMatchups.title: Houston's offensive glass against a weak DRB
keyMatchups.body: Houston rebounds 32.4% of its own misses, 2nd in the league. The Clippers' DRB % ranks 23rd. Second chances for the Rockets' 2nd-ranked offense could decide the final game of the week before shooting does.

weekAhead.watch: Whether the turnover rate drops against a slate of teams that mostly don't force turnovers. If the Clippers still give the ball away against Utah and San Antonio, the 15.7 TOV % is a habit, not a blip.

restOfSeason.body: The 4-8 start is an honest one, so the outlook rests on what changes rather than on luck evening out. The three-point shooting should drift down toward the 37-38% range this franchise has lived in. The turnover rate should also come back toward its old 13% neighborhood. Those roughly cancel, which leaves the offense somewhere near league average. The defense is the anchor: rim protection and defensive rebounding have been weak for two seasons now. Nothing on the roster other than Lopez suggests that is about to turn. I expect the margin to tighten modestly from -4.1 but stay negative, for a final total of roughly 30 to 36 wins. That sits at or below the fringe of the Western play-in picture.
swingFactors: Turnover rate returning to its historical range
Rim protection and rebounding from the frontcourt beyond Lopez
Garland's impact catching up to his usage

confidence.note: Only 12 games, but the rebounding and defensive weaknesses match last season's profile.
